steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) are more and more recognized as important in modern cryptography, as cryptographic communities try to address some of the most significant challenges of the blockchain: privacy and scalability. It is also the essential technique in Zcash. From the perspective of both users and developers, the higher emphasis on information privacy and security has made people appreciate the privacy advantages of zero-knowledge proofs more. As the usage of decentralized finance (DeFi) grows, zero-knowledge applications that give scalability and privacy advantages will have more chances to increase their adoption across the industry. But not every computational problem can be addressed directly with zero-knowledge proofs. We have to transform the problem into the correct form of computation instead. The rank-1 constraint system (R1CS) describes the execution of statements written in high-level programming languages and many ZKP applications use it, but there is no standard way of representing them. Circom is a novel domain-specific language for transforming computational problems into R1CS format circuits. In the specific process of a first-order zero-knowledge proof, we first convert the problem into a computational problem in Circom and then into R1CS format circuits.

Because the R1CS representation is flexible and program organizations and compiler optimization levels vary, the compiled R1CS forms generated from circuit language programs with the same underlying semantics can be significantly different, and this makes further analysis and verification of ZKP programs difficult.

In this paper we propose a data-flow-based algorithm for generating a normalization of R1CS, which converts different R1CS constraints into a normal form and makes it easier to determine equivalence and correctness. To do this, the algorithm first transforms an R1CS into a data flow graph structure that resembles an expression tree. Then it segments and abstracts the data flow graph, which removes differences between equivalent R1CS constraints that may come from the generation process. Finally we propose sorting rules to sort the constraints and variables in the R1CS, and in the end this gives a unique normal form for equivalent R1CS.

- Causes, benchmark, contributions
  - classify/summarize reasons and characteristics of equivalent R1CS (mainstream compilers' constraint generation logic, R1CS expressiveness)
  - relatively complete benchmark from these reasons; algorithm passes all test cases -> unique identical canonical form
  - contribution to R1CS optimization: removes redundancy, normalizes representation, improves existing methods, eases equivalence/correctness analysis; shown by benchmark

## Related Work

- Eli et al.: zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument (SNARG) R1CS
- historically focus on satisfiability; prover incurs finite field operations for an n-sized R1CS instance
- Alexander et al.: Brakedown, first built system with linear-time SNARKs for NP
- Circom / R1CS as before/after compilation -> semantic consistency in compilation
- compilation paradigms in other languages: data flow, syntax tree, semantic mapping
- R1CS form constraints -> data flow as starting point

## Paper Organization

- next section: preliminaries; Section 3: algorithm process; Section 4: critical steps, formal description; Section 5: benchmarks and results; Section 6: conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) are more and more recognized as important in modern cryptography, as cryptographic communities try to address some of the most significant challenges of the blockchain: privacy and scalability. It is also the essential technique in Zcash. From the perspective of both users and developers, the higher emphasis on information privacy and security has made people appreciate the privacy advantages of zero-knowledge proofs more. As the usage of decentralized finance (DeFi) grows, zero-knowledge applications that give scalability and privacy advantages will have more chances to increase their adoption across the industry. But not every computational problem can be addressed directly with zero-knowledge proofs. We have to transform the problem into the correct form of computation instead. The rank-1 constraint system (R1CS) describes the execution of statements written in high-level programming languages and many ZKP applications use it, but there is no standard way of representing them. Circom is a novel domain-specific language for transforming computational problems into R1CS format circuits. In the specific process of a first-order zero-knowledge proof, we first convert the problem into a computational problem in Circom and then into R1CS format circuits.

Because the R1CS representation is flexible and program organizations and compiler optimization levels vary, the compiled R1CS forms generated from circuit language programs with the same underlying semantics can be significantly different, and this makes further analysis and verification of ZKP programs difficult.

In this paper we propose a data-flow-based algorithm for generating a normalization of R1CS, which converts different R1CS constraints into a normal form and makes it easier to determine equivalence and correctness. To do this, the algorithm first transforms an R1CS into a data flow graph structure that resembles an expression tree. Then it segments and abstracts the data flow graph, which removes differences between equivalent R1CS constraints that may come from the generation process. Finally we propose sorting rules to sort the constraints and variables in the R1CS, and in the end this gives a unique normal form for equivalent R1CS.

We also classify and summarize the reasons for and characteristics of the different equivalent R1CS that are generated, based on the constraint generation logic of mainstream compilers and on the expressiveness of R1CS. Based on these reasons for producing equivalent R1CS, we also create a relatively complete benchmark. Our algorithm passes all test cases in the benchmark, which shows that equivalent R1CS can be converted into a unique and identical canonical form under various circumstances.

This work contributes to R1CS optimization with a novel algorithm for generating canonical forms of equivalent R1CS constraints. Our algorithm can remove unnecessary redundancy and normalize the representation, so it can improve existing methods and it makes the analysis of equivalence and correctness easier. The effectiveness and practicality of the algorithm are also demonstrated by our comprehensive benchmark.

## Related Work

Eli et al. design, implement and evaluate a zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument (SNARG) R1CS. Historically, research on the factors associated with R1CS has focused on satisfiability. In another paper, the prover incurs finite field operations to prove the satisfiability of an n-sized R1CS instance. Alexander et al. introduce Brakedown, which is the first built system that provides linear-time SNARKs for NP.

If we consider Circom and R1CS format circuits as two languages before and after compilation, research on generating the R1CS paradigm is more like research on semantic consistency in compilation. At present, patent applications and research papers propose ideas and solutions for generating compilation paradigms in other languages, and they mainly explore data flow, syntax tree or semantic mapping aspects. These studies give important insights into the fundamental information that semantically identical programs carry in the compilation process. But because of the constraints built into the R1CS form, this paper in the end chooses data flow as the starting point for the research.

## Paper Organization

The paper is organized as follows. The next section gives a brief preliminary review of zero-knowledge proof and related tools. Section 3 gives the process of the algorithm proposed in this paper. Section 4 explains in detail the logic of the critical steps and their formal description. Section 5 presents the specific categories of benchmarks and the corresponding experimental results. Finally, Section 6 concludes the study.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) are increasingly recognized for their importance in modern cryptography [1], as more and more cryptographic communities seek to address some of the blockchain's most significant challenges: privacy and scalability. It is also the essential technique in Zcash [2,3]. From both users' and developers' perspectives, the heightened emphasis on information privacy and security has led to a greater appreciation of the privacy advantages offered by zero-knowledge proofs. As decentralized finance (DeFi) usage grows, zero-knowledge applications that provide scalability and privacy advantages will have more opportunities to increase industry-wide adoption. However, not all computational problems can be directly addressed using zero-knowledge proofs. Instead, we must transform the problem into the correct form of computation. The rank-1 constraint system (R1CS) describes the execution of statements written in high-level programming languages and is used by many ZKP applications, but there is no standard way of representing them [4]. Circom is a novel domain-specific language for transforming computational problems into R1CS format circuits. [5] In the specific process of a first-order zero-knowledge proof, we first convert the problem into a computational problem in Circom, and then into R1CS format circuits.

Due to the flexible nature of R1CS representation and the variation of program organizations and compiler optimization levels, there can be significant differences in the compiled R1CS forms generated from circuit language programs with the same underlying semantics, which leads to difficulties in further ZKP program analysis and verification.

This paper proposes a data-flow-based algorithm for generating a normalization of R1CS, enabling the conversion of different R1CS constraints into a normal form and facilitating the determination of equivalence and correctness. To achieve this, the algorithm starts by transforming an R1CS into a data flow graph structure resembling an expression tree. It then segments and abstracts the data flow graph, eliminating differences between equivalent R1CS constraints that may arise from the generation process. Finally, sorting rules are proposed to sort the constraints and variables within the R1CS, resulting in a unique normal form for equivalent R1CS.

Moreover, we classify and summarize the reasons for and characteristics of the different equivalent R1CS generated, based on the constraint generation logic of mainstream compilers and the expressiveness of R1CS. In addition, based on the identified reasons for producing equivalent R1CS, we create a relatively complete benchmark. Our proposed algorithm, which passes all test cases in the benchmark, demonstrates that equivalent R1CS can be converted into a unique and identical canonical form under various circumstances.

This work contributes to R1CS optimization by providing a novel algorithm for generating canonical forms of equivalent R1CS constraints. Our algorithm can eliminate unnecessary redundancy and normalize the representation; thus it can improve existing methods and facilitates the analysis of equivalence and correctness. Furthermore, the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed algorithm are demonstrated through our comprehensive benchmark.

## Related Work

Eli et al. design, implement, and evaluate a zero-knowledge succinct non-interactive argument (SNARG) R1CS [6]. Historically, research investigating the factors associated with R1CS has focused on satisfiability. In [7], the prover incurs finite field operations to prove the satisfiability of an n-sized R1CS instance [7]. Alexander et al. introduce Brakedown, the first built system that provides linear-time SNARKs for NP [8].

Considering Circom and R1CS format circuits as two languages before and after compilation, research on the generation of the R1CS paradigm is closer to research on semantic consistency in compilation. Currently, patent applications and research papers propose ideas and solutions for generating compilation paradigms in other languages, mainly exploring data flow [9], syntax tree [10], or semantic mapping [11] aspects. These studies offer crucial insights into the fundamental information that semantically identical programs carry in the compilation process. However, due to the inherent constraints embedded in the R1CS form, this paper ultimately chooses data flow as the starting point for research.

## Paper Organization

The paper is organized as follows. The next section gives a brief preliminary review of zero-knowledge proof and related tools. Section 3 provides the process of the algorithm proposed in this paper. The technical exposition in Section 4 explains in detail the logic of the critical steps and their formal description. Section 5 presents the specific categories of benchmarks and their corresponding experimental results. Lastly, Section 6 concludes the present study.
